## Elvator pitch/statement of work:

This report analyzes data from the Lahman Baseball Database to identify meaningful patterns and relationships in professional baseball. Using SQL queries and Python-based analysis, the project explores player salaries, batting performance, team spending strategies, positional salary differences, and career longevity. The goal is to demonstrate how data can be used to answer real-world questions about performance, value, and strategy

By analyzing batting averages, team payrolls, and career longevity, the analysis highlights how small sample sizes can be misleading, how teams invest differently in talent, and how long-term success is difficult to achieve. The results demonstrate how data-driven insights can support smarter decision-making in sports and beyond.

"""

## QUESTION|TASK 2

__This three-part question requires you to calculate batting average (number of hits divided by the number of at-bats)__  
   This task shows how batting average becomes more meaningful as stricter at-bat requirements are applied. Players with only one at bat can appear to have perfect averages, which are misleading due to small sample sizes. Requiring at least 10 at bats produces more reliable results, and calculating career averages with a 100 at-bat minimum highlights players who performed consistently over time.


```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
query_ba1_with_ab = """
SELECT 
    playerID,
    yearID,
    SUM(AB) AS total_at_bats,
    CAST(SUM(H) AS FLOAT)/SUM(AB) AS batting_average
FROM batting
WHERE AB > 0
GROUP BY playerID, yearID
ORDER BY batting_average DESC, playerID
LIMIT 5;
"""

pd.read_sql(query_ba1_with_ab, con)
```

```{python}
query_ba2_with_ab = """
SELECT 
    playerID,
    yearID,
    SUM(AB) AS total_at_bats,
    CAST(SUM(H) AS FLOAT)/SUM(AB) AS batting_average
FROM batting
GROUP BY playerID, yearID
HAVING SUM(AB) >= 10
ORDER BY batting_average DESC, playerID
LIMIT 5;
"""

pd.read_sql(query_ba2_with_ab, con)

```

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
query_ba3 = """
SELECT 
    playerID,
    CAST(SUM(H) AS FLOAT)/SUM(AB) AS career_batting_average,
    SUM(AB) AS total_at_bats
FROM batting
GROUP BY playerID
HAVING SUM(AB) >= 100
ORDER BY career_batting_average DESC
LIMIT 5;
"""

pd.read_sql(query_ba3, con)

```


## QUESTION|TASK 3

__Pick any two baseball teams and compare them using a metric of your choice (average salary, home runs, number of wins, etc). Write an SQL query to get the data you need, then make a graph using Lets-Plot to visualize the comparison. What do you learn?__

I chose average player salary as the comparison metric because it provides a clear measure of how much each team is willing and able to invest in talent. The comparison between the New York Yankees and the Oakland Athletics shows a consistent and substantial difference in spending across seasons. The Yankees maintain significantly higher average salaries, especially in later years, reflecting a strategy focused on financial investment to acquire and retain top players. In contrast, the Athletics operate with much lower salaries, emphasizing efficiency, player development, and cost-effective roster construction. This comparison highlights how salary influences team-building strategies while also showing that higher spending does not automatically guarantee greater on-field success.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
query_team_salary = """
SELECT
    yearID,
    teamID,
    AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM salaries
WHERE teamID IN ('NYA', 'OAK')
GROUP BY yearID, teamID
ORDER BY yearID;
"""

team_salary = pd.read_sql(query_team_salary, con)
team_salary
```

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
from lets_plot import *
LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

ggplot(team_salary, aes(x='yearID', y='avg_salary', color='teamID')) + \

    labs(
        title='Average Player Salary Over Time',
        x='Year',
        y='Average Salary (USD)',
        color='Team'
    ) + \
    theme_minimal()

```

## STRETCH QUESTION|TASK 1

__Advanced Salary Distribution by Position (with Case Statement):__  

This analysis looks at how player salaries differ by position, assigning each player’s salary to the position they played the most in a given season. The results show that some positions, such as pitchers and key infield roles, tend to earn higher average and maximum salaries, reflecting how valuable and in-demand these roles are. Other positions fall into lower salary categories, which suggests they are either more specialized or easier for teams to replace. Overall, the table highlights how teams distribute money differently depending on position and reinforces the idea that salary is closely tied to how teams value certain roles on the field.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
query_position_salary = """
WITH primary_position AS (
    SELECT
        f.playerID,
        f.yearID,
        f.POS AS position,
        SUM(f.G) AS games_played,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY f.playerID, f.yearID
            ORDER BY SUM(f.G) DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM fielding f
    GROUP BY f.playerID, f.yearID, f.POS
),
player_position AS (
    SELECT
        playerID,
        yearID,
        position
    FROM primary_position
    WHERE rn = 1
)
SELECT
    pp.position,
    AVG(s.salary) AS average_salary,
    COUNT(DISTINCT s.playerID) AS total_players,
    MAX(s.salary) AS highest_salary,
    CASE
        WHEN AVG(s.salary) > 3000000 THEN 'High Salary'
        WHEN AVG(s.salary) BETWEEN 2000000 AND 3000000 THEN 'Medium Salary'
        ELSE 'Low Salary'
    END AS salary_category
FROM player_position pp
JOIN salaries s
    ON pp.playerID = s.playerID
   AND pp.yearID = s.yearID
GROUP BY pp.position
ORDER BY average_salary DESC;
"""

pd.read_sql(query_position_salary, con)

```


## STRETCH QUESTION|TASK 2

__Advanced Career Longevity and Performance (with Subqueries):__

This analysis examines career longevity for players who appeared in at least 10 games, ensuring that only meaningful careers are included. Career length was calculated as the difference between a player’s first and last recorded seasons. The results show that a small group of players managed exceptionally long careers spanning many years, highlighting consistency, durability, and sustained performance at the professional level. In contrast, the average career length is much shorter, reinforcing how difficult it is for most players to remain in the league for extended periods of time.

```{python}
# Include and execute your code here
query_career_length = """
WITH player_games AS (
    SELECT
        playerID,
        SUM(G) AS total_games
    FROM batting
    GROUP BY playerID
    HAVING SUM(G) >= 10
),
career_lengths AS (
    SELECT
        b.playerID,
        MIN(b.yearID) AS first_year,
        MAX(b.yearID) AS last_year,
        MAX(b.yearID) - MIN(b.yearID) AS career_length
    FROM batting b
    JOIN player_games pg
        ON b.playerID = pg.playerID
    GROUP BY b.playerID
)
SELECT
    cl.playerID,
    p.nameFirst AS first_name,
    p.nameLast AS last_name,
    cl.career_length
FROM career_lengths cl
JOIN people p
    ON cl.playerID = p.playerID
ORDER BY cl.career_length DESC
LIMIT 10;
"""

pd.read_sql(query_career_length, con)

```
